pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 📝 **Strand 2 — Productivity Software**
Sub-strand 3: Introduction to Desktop Publishing

Professional designers create, review and improve. In this unit you will produce a four-page publication, exchange it with a classmate, describe it, and evaluate it against agreed criteria.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B9.2.3.1** Critique a desktop published document.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B9.2.3.1.1** Create and present a desktop published document (flyer, advertisement, invitation card, business card).
- **B9.2.3.1.2** Describe a desktop published document.
- **B9.2.3.1.3** Evaluate a desktop published document.

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 6.1 Creating a Four-Page Publication with Images and Overflow

- 6.3 Evaluating a Desktop Published Document

**Core competencies developed:** Creativity and Innovation (CI5.4), Digital Literacy (DL5.1), Communication and Collaboration (CC9.6), Critical Thinking (CP5.1).

lessons.title: Creating a Four-Page Publication with Images and Overflow

pages.title: Creating a Four-Page Publication with Images and Overflow
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.2.3.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- create and present a four-page document with images and text overflow.
A multi-page publication such as a **storybook**, **brochure**, **school magazine** or **newsletter** usually has more text than fits in one text box. DTP software handles this with **text overflow**: the extra text flows into **linked (connected) text boxes** on the same or following pages.
> 🪜 **Step by step — Building a four-page storybook or newsletter**
1. Choose a template (e.g. **Newsletter** or **Booklet**) or a blank A4/A5 page; add pages until you have four (**Insert › Page**).
2. Plan the layout: page 1 cover (title, picture, author); pages 2–3 the main content; page 4 back cover or contacts.
3. Use **Master Pages** (View › Master Page) for repeating items such as page numbers and the school logo.
4. Draw a text box on page 2 and paste or type a long story. When the overflow indicator appears, click it and then click in a text box on page 3 to **link** them; repeat as needed.
5. Insert at least one picture per page and set **Wrap Text** (Square or Tight) so text flows around it.
6. Check spelling, then save as .pub (or .docx) and **export as PDF** for printing or sharing.

pages.title: Describing a Desktop Published Document
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.2.3.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- exchange documents with a classmate;
- describe a document in terms of text and image position, colour, mechanics and content accuracy.
| **Aspect to describe** | **Guiding questions** |
|---|---|
| Purpose and audience | What type of publication is it? Who is it for? |
| Position of text and images | Where are the headline, body text and pictures placed? Is there a clear starting point? |
| Use of colour | Which colours are used? Do they match and contrast well? |
| Typography | Which fonts and sizes? How many fonts? |
| Mechanics | Punctuation, spelling, italics, capitalisation and grammar |
| Content accuracy | Are facts, names, dates, prices and contacts correct and complete? |

pages.title: Evaluating a Desktop Published Document
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.2.3.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- evaluate a document using set criteria;
- give constructive feedback.
| **Criterion** | **4 – Excellent** | **3 – Good** | **2 – Fair** | **1 – Needs work** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Position of text and images | Balanced, aligned, clear reading order | Mostly balanced | Some crowding | Cluttered or confusing |
| General layout | Consistent margins, white space, master items | Mostly consistent | Inconsistent | No clear layout |
| Use of colour | Harmonious, high contrast, purposeful | Good | Some clashes | Hard to read |
| Mechanics | No errors | 1–2 errors | 3–5 errors | Many errors |
| Appropriateness for purpose | Perfectly suits audience and purpose | Suits | Partly suits | Does not suit |
> 🧪 **Activity — Peer critique**
Give your document to the learner assigned to you and collect theirs. Score it with the rubric, then write **two strengths** (“I like how…”), **two improvements** (“You could…”) and **one question**. Return it, discuss politely, then improve your own document based on the feedback you received.

pages.body:

## Short answer questions
1. Explain how to link text boxes so that text flows from page 2 to page 3.
2. List **five** criteria for evaluating a desktop published document.
3. Why is peer critique useful in design?
